subject: Cloud Computing
title: Mainframes: The First Shared Computers
description: A fast breakdown of Mainframes: The First Shared Computers for builders.

hook.text: In the 1960s, one computer filled a room. Hundreds of people shared it through terminals.

buildup.text: IBM's mainframes dominated business. Companies rented them because buying one cost millions.

discovery.text: Users connected via dumb terminals — screens with no processing power of their own.

twist.text: This sounds ancient, but it's the same model as today's cloud: many users, one powerful machine.

climax.text: Mainframes never died. Banks and airlines still run critical systems on them right now.

punchline.text: The cloud isn't new. It's mainframes with better marketing.

quiz.question: How does the mainframe model relate to modern cloud computing?
options: Both share a powerful central machine among many users
Mainframes and cloud have nothing in common
Mainframes were personal computers for individual use

details.summary: Mainframes in the 1950s and 60s were the first shared computers, allowing multiple users to access a single powerful machine through terminals. They introduced concepts like resource sharing, job scheduling, and centralized management that would later define cloud computing.
details.whyItMatters: Every modern cloud concept traces back to mainframes. Understanding this origin reveals that cloud computing is not a new idea but the evolution of decades-old shared computing principles.
takeaways: Mainframes let multiple users share one powerful computer
They introduced resource scheduling and centralized management
Cloud computing descends directly from mainframe concepts

faq.question: How did mainframes work?
faq.answer: A mainframe was a large centralized computer accessed through connected terminals. Users submitted jobs that the mainframe processed in batches or through time-sharing. The mainframe managed resources, security, and scheduling, much like a cloud provider does today.

faq.question: What companies made early mainframes?
faq.answer: IBM dominated the mainframe market with its System/360 series. Other significant manufacturers included UNIVAC, Burroughs, Honeywell, and CDC. IBM mainframes became so dominant that competitors were collectively called the BUNCH.
